name: Electrolysis

image.caption: 20180908 1054 - Claire's FFS - 11 - day 5 - Claire, electrolysis patient, Carolyn - 51541040

lead: Electrolysis clears unwanted hair for good, from stray facial hairs and brow edges to a cleaner hairline and body hair. It works on any hair colour and skin tone, including the light or grey hair that laser handles poorly.

A practitioner slides a fine probe into each follicle and applies current to destroy its growth centre, so the treated hair stops returning. Galvanic methods use a chemical reaction, thermolysis uses heat from high-frequency current, and blend methods combine both. It has been practised in the US since 1875 and is the method the FDA recognises for permanent hair removal.

paras: Each hair is treated one at a time, so small areas like brows, hairlines or stray facial hairs are done in repeated short sessions. Courses can run 12 to 18 months or more, with treated areas clearing gradually across visits.

Short-lived redness, swelling and scabbing are common. Infection and scarring are rare and linked to poor technique or sterilisation, with higher scarring risk in keloid-prone skin. Practitioner licensing varies by US state.

chain: Permanently clear skin or cleaner hairline
angle.text: Electrolysis gets rid of facial, brow, hairline or body hair permanently, on any hair colour. A fine probe and current destroy each follicle's growth centre, so treated hairs stop coming back and the area clears over many sessions.

lead: Electrolysis, in appearance contexts, is a hair-removal method in which a practitioner inserts a fine sterile probe into each hair follicle and applies electrical current to destroy the follicle's growth centre. People use it to shape a hairline, clean up brows, remove stray facial hair and clear beard-area hair, and it is distinct from the chemistry process of the same name [1][2].

It works on any hair colour and skin tone, which is the reason many people choose it where laser or light devices are less suited, such as light, grey or white hair. Wikipedia's hair-removal article describes electrolysis (electrology) as practised in the United States since 1875 and as the method it identifies as recognised by the FDA for permanent hair removal [3]. A 2021 literature review of hair-removal practices likewise lists electrolysis as the one epilation method described as permanent, with the other methods described as temporary [4].

Treatment is done one follicle at a time, so courses for larger areas commonly run for many months or longer [2]. People who have used it describe a trade: a slow, per-hair process in exchange for results that do not depend on hair colour [5]. In practice the same method is also used to clear hair from reconstructed tissue and in gender-affirming care, where clients commonly seek facial hair clearance over many months.[6][2]
infobox: Often 15 to 30 sessions over 12 to 18 months for small to medium areas [2]
About $50 to $150 per hour, higher in some cities [2]
Galvanic roughly 10-60 seconds; thermolysis roughly 1-5 seconds [2]
Needle epilators proposed as Class II devices; about 31 states license electrologists [2]
Laser and intense pulsed light, approved by the FDA from 1997 [3][8]

paras: Grokipedia describes three approaches. Galvanic electrolysis uses direct current to generate sodium hydroxide in the follicle and is slower, at roughly 10 to 60 seconds per follicle. Thermolysis uses high-frequency current to heat the follicle, at roughly 1 to 5 seconds per follicle, and may have higher regrowth rates. Blend combines the two and takes longer per hair but is used for stubborn or curved hairs [2].

Wikipedia's electrology article gives further technical detail: galvanic current is typically in the range of 0 to 3 milliamperes and works through the alkali produced at the probe, while thermolysis, also called radio-frequency or short-wave, operates at 13.56 MHz and heats matrix cells to roughly 48 to 50 degrees Celsius so that they coagulate [7]. It states that all three methods, when properly performed, can destroy the hair matrix and that none is inherently better, with outcomes depending on operator skill, hair type, skin condition and the client's pain threshold [7].

In technique, the probe is slid down alongside the hair in the direction of growth to the level of the matrix, current is applied, and the loosened hair is lifted out. Practitioners start at low power and adjust upward, lowering it if the client finds it too uncomfortable [7].

Before treatment, Grokipedia describes a consultation covering medical history, medications and contraindications such as pregnancy, pacemakers, active infection, keloid tendency and recent isotretinoin use, with clients usually shaving 24 to 48 hours beforehand. Probes are ideally single-use and each follicle is treated under magnification.[2] Areas commonly treated include the face, eyebrows, nose bridge, outer ear, underarms, bikini line and legs; the page notes that it is not recommended inside the nostrils or ear canal.[2] Newer devices offer touchscreen settings and insulated probes intended to localise heat and reduce pain.[2]

According to Grokipedia, St. Louis ophthalmologist Charles E. Michel introduced electrolysis in 1875 to treat ingrown eyelashes. Paul M. Kree patented a multiple-needle epilator in 1916, thermolysis was described in the 1920s, and a blend method followed, with sources giving conflicting dates in the 1930s and 1940s. Transistor machines in the 1970s and multi-probe systems in the 1980s later improved speed and precision [2].

Wikipedia's electrology article credits Henri Bordier with first reporting thermolysis in the medical literature in 1924 and Arthur Hinkel with developing the blend method in 1948, with a book by Hinkel and R. W. Lind following in 1968 [7]. The same article notes that laser hair removal arrived in the 1990s and that the FDA's position is that lasers can claim only to reduce hair growth [7].

Hobbyist interest has also appeared in technical communities. In 2026 a Hacker News post about a home-built electrolysis machine drew dozens of comments from people describing professional treatment, cost and scarring risk [5].

Grokipedia cites a success rate of about 93 percent attributed to the American Academy of Dermatology and says some regrowth is seen in roughly 15 to 40 percent of cases, which it notes sits uneasily with the word permanent [2]. It also reports that hormonal conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome can require more sessions, and that laser and IPL are less effective on light, grey or white hair, a point electrolysis proponents emphasise [2].

Hairs grow in cycles, so follicles in the resting phase are not visible at a given session; practitioners therefore repeat treatment at intervals, and a single hair may need several passes, according to commenters describing their experience [5]. Wikipedia states that laser hair removal has been FDA-approved since 1997 and sometimes becomes permanent after several sessions, whereas it identifies electrology as the method recognised for permanent removal [3]. A 2000 study of 12 patients cited in Wikipedia's laser article found laser to be about 60 times faster than galvanic electrolysis, though its authors noted that not all modern electrolysis methods were tested [8].

Commenters describe speed as a limiting factor. One estimated roughly three to four hairs per minute for a home-built device, similar to many professionals, while noting that a very skilled operator can be faster [5].

A 2024 review of best practices for gender-affirming laser hair removal states that electrolysis and laser are both effective for permanent hair reduction, that laser is less painful, and that hair removal in this setting reduces surgical complications and gender dysphoria while insurance coverage is inconsistent.[6] Wikipedia's laser article states that lasers target melanin and respond poorly to white, light blonde, strawberry blonde, grey and fine vellus hair, and that the FDA uses 'permanent hair reduction' to mean a long-term, stable decrease in the number of hairs that regrow, not necessarily complete removal.[8] Grokipedia describes laser and IPL as typically reaching 70 to 90 percent reduction.[2]

sections.h: Comparison with laser and other methods
paras: The 2021 Skin Therapy Letter review divides hair removal into depilation, which removes the shaft (shaving, chemical depilatories), and epilation, which removes the shaft, follicle and bulb (plucking, threading, waxing, sugaring, lasers, intense pulsed light, electrolysis and photodynamic therapy). Its abstract states that all methods are temporary except electrolysis.[4]

Wikipedia reports that laser hair removal was tested experimentally for about twenty years, became commercially available in 1995-1996 and was approved by the FDA in 1997, and that a 2006 Cochrane meta-analysis reported about 50 percent reduction for up to six months with alexandrite and diode lasers.[8][3] It also cites a 2000 study of 12 patients in Ankara in which alexandrite laser was about 60 times faster, less painful and more reliable than galvanic electrolysis, noting that the study did not test every modern form of electrolysis.[8] Wikipedia also notes that many sold methods, such as electric tweezers and non-prescription hair inhibitors, lack published clinical proof.[3]

Grokipedia lists eflornithine cream as an FDA-approved topical that slows facial hair growth and is used alongside other methods, and reports that electrolysis reduces regrowth cumulatively where shaving and waxing need repeating.[2][4]

Electrolysis is widely used by transgender and gender-diverse clients for facial and body hair, and Grokipedia says satisfaction is high, with clients reporting greater confidence and less dysphoria, while the long time commitment and discomfort are common complaints.[2] A 2025 cross-sectional study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology examined permanent hair removal in gender-diverse adults assigned male at birth.[6] A 2026 paper examined the number of electrolysis sessions and length of treatment needed for surgical readiness before genital gender-affirming surgery.[6]

Case reports describe electrolysis for hair inside the body after reconstruction, such as follicles along the urethral plate before staged urethroplasty in a transgender man, and intraoral hair after nasolabial flap reconstruction in two patients, where laser was not feasible; both patients improved, one with slight recurrence needing a second session.[6] A 2026 review of hair removal in paramedian forehead flaps lists electrolysis among durable methods but states that laser remains the primary method for most flap applications.[6] A 2025 pilot study of blend electrolysis in three beagles reported reduced density or complete alopecia lasting at least three months and described the method as feasible but time-intensive.[6]

Commonly reported effects are redness, swelling and pinpoint scabbing lasting about one to three days, with stinging or pricking during treatment. Rare effects include infection, usually linked to poor sterilization, and scarring, mainly in people with keloid-prone skin or from improper technique. Grokipedia lists active infection, keloid history, recent isotretinoin use, pregnancy and pacemakers as contraindications in some practice guidance [2].

People who have been treated describe the sensation in varied terms: one commenter compared it to tweezing repeated hundreds of times per session, another to a small shock or twinge per hair, and one forum user described the first full-session experience as like being snapped with a rubber band [5][9]. Commenters stress that operator skill governs both discomfort and scarring [5].

Grokipedia reports that the FDA proposed in 1982 to classify needle-type epilators as Class II devices requiring 510(k) clearance, that about 31 US states and the District of Columbia license electrologists with training requirements ranging from roughly 300 to 1,100 hours, and that a voluntary Certified Professional Electrologist credential exists [2]. Wikipedia likewise notes that many US states require training and licensing [7].

Grokipedia says insurance generally treats electrolysis as cosmetic, though some plans cover medically necessary cases such as hirsutism or gender-affirming care, and that access is limited in rural areas.[2] Wikipedia notes that certification and licensing information is maintained by bodies such as the American Electrology Association.[7]

Electrolysis is discussed in appearance communities as a way to reshape the hairline or brows, clear stray facial hair in people whose hair is too light for laser, and treat beard-area hair. Cost and treatment length are common topics, with Grokipedia citing full facial treatment as roughly $1,000 to $10,000 or more over one to two years [2]. Insurance generally treats it as cosmetic, with exceptions for medical need such as hirsutism or gender-affirming care [2].

Users discuss it alongside other permanent-reduction options. One person in a T Nation log thread described a series of sessions on the upper body, and another noted disappointment after six sessions when hair seemed weaker but still present, illustrating how individual results are reported to vary [9][10]. A commenter on Hacker News who had paid for facial and neck treatment described spending very large amounts over 100 to 300 hours at about $100 per hour [5].

No studies of electrolysis hair removal specifically have been found. Registered trials under the name electrolysis concern percutaneous electrolysis therapy for tendon and muscle conditions, which is a different technique [11]. Comparative evidence for hair removal is discussed mainly for laser and light devices, including a 2006 Cochrane analysis cited by Wikipedia that reported about 50 percent reduction for up to six months with alexandrite and diode lasers [3].

The 2021 Skin Therapy Letter review covers hair-removal practices broadly, dividing them into depilation and epilation, and describes electrolysis as the permanent option among them, alongside eflornithine cream as an FDA-approved product that slows facial hair growth when combined with other methods [4].

lore.intro: Electrolysis is discussed as the slow-but-colour-blind option for hairlines, brows and facial hair, with cost and number of sessions the main topics [5][9].
